items.title: Converting SCORM to PPT
items.summary: I am creating educational content. The tool of my company can export this as a SCORM file, but nothing else. Since I don't want to do the work twice, I'd like to convert the SCORM file as PPT. At the moment, I'm very new to SCORM, so I don't have any particular idea on which features of SCORM need to be supported. Very basic support is sufficient for now. Requirements: Works on Windows (Windows 10+) is gratis (Open Source preferred) works offline (no upload to the Internet)

Since I don't want to do the work twice, I'd like to convert the SCORM file as PPT. At the moment, I'm very new to SCORM, so I don't have any particular idea on which features of SCORM need to be supported. Very basic support is sufficient for now. Requirements: Works on Windows (Windows 10+) is gratis (Open Source preferred) works offline (no upload to the Internet)

comments.text: Converting a SCORM file to a PowerPoint presentation (PPT) can be a bit challenging because SCORM is a package format used for e-learning content, while PowerPoint is a presentation format. However, there are some open-source tools that can help you extract the content from the SCORM package and convert it to a more readable format, which you can then use to create a PowerPoint presentation manually. One tool that meets your requirements is the SCORM Cloud Player, which is an open-source project hosted on GitHub. Here are the steps to use it: Download the SCORM Cloud Player from the GitHub repository: https://github.com/cyber-kube/scorm-cloud-player Extract the downloaded ZIP file to a folder on your Windows computer. Open the extracted folder and locate the "scorm-cloud-player.html" file. Double-click on the "scorm-cloud-player.html" file to open it in your default web browser.

items.title: WYSIWYG editor for Jetpack Compose?
items.summary: We used to use Matisse on our team to make mock ups and even generate the initial code for Swing user interfaces. I'm investigating moving to Jetpack Compose and one of the hot questions is, where is the WYSIWYG editor for Compose? Something basic which will take care of component layouts and spacing for us, and export to code at the end. Live editing of the view after the fact would be amazing, but is out of scope. I had a bit of a play with Figma, but the usability was extremely poor compared to Matisse and can't seem to do much of anything without plugins.

items.title: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel
items.summary: Hi HN! I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious. So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.

deep.body: Hi HN! I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious. So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves. I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging ( https://declarative-dragging.github.io/ ) on the front page of HN and the spark came back! It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions. A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges there I'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance

comments.text: Could you drop a link to the repo? Would love to contribute to this...

In chapter 3 "pull a term out of the exponent" I'm not finding a way to do it: I can drag a term around within the exponent, and that sum will rearrange when I do, but if I try to drop it outside the exponent, it only snaps back into place.

This is super compelling. For my learning style, everything was very intuitive, and dare I say fun. I think this can open up math for a whole segment of the learner population that previously did not enjoy engaging with it! Great work.
log and exp could use more of an intro I think. Very cool and great idea!

> It can only move in ways the maths allows. This property is desirable for a tool that assists you in performing work, but actually undesirable for a tool designed to guide your learning: it means you are protected from doing something wrong (much like when they put up the bumpers/siderails at a bowling alley), the result being that you receive no feedback when your mental model requires adjustment.

The section on a product of binomials breaks for me. After dragging one binomial onto the other, the resulting products of a term times a binomial can't be distributed. That is, I get a product like (1+t)t but I can't drag the t without moving the whole expression. https://dragdropmath.com/#/c/brackets

The solutions do weird stuff like moving a term back and forth across the equal sign uselessly. It doesn't seem possible to complete the square or to square the sides of an equality, quite awkard for solving quadratics Also, the UI gives no indication of how the operations are triggered. Needs a way to see what operations are possible and how to execute them.

I don't think this works well, in its current state. I mainly think its to do with the drag and drop functionality itself - it becomes somewhat unintuitive and even with knowledge of what should or could be possible I struggle to achieve my goals. A few more iterations of that, particularly with some over the shoulder observations of your target audience, might help significantly.

items.title: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
items.summary: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people.

deep.body: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

comments.text: Surprising fun and awesome! Love it. It was not immediately clear how the game was played but it came to me soon enough. I think one or two "trial/tutorial" rounds would go a long way to give me a proper shot at the leaderboard. I wasted my first 2-3 balls as I was looking at the UI trying to understand how to play.
bouncemarket: bought Right x52 at avg 0.19, landed Right, +42.21 in one round https://bouncemarket.minhanhday.com/r/FYv-qiLU
This looks fun, but I imagine someone somewhere in a financial exchange company looking at this and thinking: "bouncing ball futures contracts, would be a thing to offer our sophisticated clients."
Completely ignoring the ball and just buying cheap shares is a surprisingly efficient strategy. Often I'm able to get both kinds of share for cheap, so I win regardless of the outcome.
So fun, and easy to profit, at least for a few minutes. Seems like if you played this professionally 40hrs a week full-time it would get tiring fast. Maybe there is a metaphor in there.
I'd like to see how much the market maker is making/losing.
Is there a way to sell shares before resolution?
